_note: What the evidence says about people, law by law. Each verdict is a judgment that maps experiments onto an idealized law. It is not a theorem. 'lacks' means people violate the law in some setting, which is all a counterexample needs. 'has' means people satisfy it in the typical setting; the formal law claims every setting. 'mixed' means the evidence is divided. Each entry also states its 'bridge': the unformalized assumption that connects the experiment's measure to the law. The laws are about what memory retrieves; the experiments measure reports and decisions.

certainty.summary: Items just studied can be available but not accessible: cued recall retrieves words that free recall missed.
sources: Tulving, E., & Pearlstone, Z. (1966). Availability versus accessibility of information in memory for words. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 5, 381-391.
certainty.bridge: Free and cued recall are taken to show what a probe retrieves. Recall failure is read as retrieval failure, not as a failure at report.

stability.summary: In recall, learning new material impairs old (retroactive interference). In recognition, strengthening other list items does not impair an item (the null list-strength effect).
sources: McGeoch, J. A. (1932). Forgetting and the law of disuse. Psychological Review, 39, 352-370.
Barnes, J. M., & Underwood, B. J. (1959). 'Fate' of first-list associations in transfer theory. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 58, 97-105.
Ratcliff, R., Clark, S. E., & Shiffrin, R. M. (1990). List-strength effect: I. Data and discussion. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 16, 163-178.
stability.bridge: Recall and recognition accuracy are taken as measures of an item's retrieval by itself as probe.

orderFree.summary: Recall depends on serial position (primacy and recency), so the order of study matters.
sources: Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64, 482-488.
orderFree.bridge: Free recall by serial position is taken to reflect the retrieval distribution after a given study order. The law itself concerns swapping the last two study events.

recency.summary: On an immediate test, the last items studied are recalled best. A filled delay removes the advantage, so this holds for the immediate test only.
sources: Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64, 482-488.
Glanzer, M., & Cunitz, A. R. (1966). Two storage mechanisms in free recall. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 5, 351-360.
recency.bridge: Free recall is taken to reflect probe-based retrieval. The law concerns two items equally similar to a probe; free recall has no explicit probe.

storedOnly.summary: The law concerns the representation memory returns; the experiments measure reports. Endorsing an unseen prototype as old does not show that the prototype itself was retrieved: a memory that returns a similar studied item (as discrimination and strength memory do) also calls it old. False recall of an unpresented word is stronger evidence, but it could be built by a response stage working on retrieved studied material.
storedOnly.bridge: Unformalized, and decisive here. A report must be linked to the retrieved representation by an explicit decision and response model.
sources: Posner, M. I., & Keele, S. W. (1968). On the genesis of abstract ideas. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 77, 353-363.
Roediger, H. L., & McDermott, K. B. (1995). Creating false memories: Remembering words not presented in lists. Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 21, 803-814.

determinate.summary: People's responses to the same cue vary from one occasion to another, which suggests that retrieval is not determinate. But the variation could arise in encoding, in context, or at report, so the evidence does not settle what memory itself retrieves. No source is cited here yet.
determinate.bridge: Unformalized: response variability must be separated from retrieval variability by a response model.
